old: Its deepest possible root may point to striking or beating, not the hard structure it later named.
In several Germanic languages, the word for this body part doubles as the word for 'leg.'
It's related to Old Norse beinn, meaning 'straight' — a sense preserved in the English word bain, meaning prompt or direct.
clues: This part of your anatomy traces back to an ancient root meaning 'straight,' a sense that still survives in a Scots word for prompt or in good condition.
One of the hard, rigid pieces that together form your skeleton; an adult has about 206. Some trace it even further back to a root meaning 'to hit or strike.'
A dog buries one in the yard, and you might pick one with someone over a grievance. Its German cousin Bein can also mean 'leg.'
